1.title: Find the traceability problem worth solving
1.intro: Food traceability means knowing where every ingredient came from and where it went. A shared record can speed recalls and prove claims such as organic or local.
pts: List what goes wrong today: slow recalls, paper records, disputed origin claims, waste from over-recalling.
Map one product chain from farm to plate: grower, packer, distributor, restaurant. Mark who writes records and who reads them.
A shared ledger helps only when several parties must trust one record and no single party should control it. If one firm controls the chain, a normal database is simpler and cheaper.
Write the question for a buyer: which problem costs you most each year, and what would you pay to cut it?
1.ex: A restaurant group recalls all romaine for 5 days because origin is unclear, costing about 18,000 in lost sales. Batch-level records would recall only two lots. Teaching figures in CAD.
1.act: Map one real chain and decide, with reasons, whether a shared ledger beats a normal database.
1.std: The decision names who writes, who reads and who pays.

2.title: Know food, data and finance rules
2.intro: Food and software rules both apply.
pts: Food safety law requires traceability one step back and one step forward for many foods; check the current federal rule for your products.
Labels and claims such as organic, local or fair-trade need certification and proof.
Privacy law applies to any personal data on staff or customers stored in records; do not place personal data on a ledger that cannot be erased.
If a token or coin is involved, securities and money-services rules may apply; get advice before you issue anything.
2.ex: Row: 'Claim organic on a menu | federal labelling rules and certifier | show certificate and lot link | before printing | certificate copy filed'.
2.act: Build a rules table for a six-restaurant pilot.

3.title: Design the record and the data capture
3.intro: Good traceability starts with simple capture at each hand-over.
pts: Define the minimum record: lot code, product, quantity, date, from, to, temperature if cold chain.
Use barcodes or QR codes on cases; test that a phone camera reads them on a wet, cold case.
Decide the ledger design: who runs the nodes, who can write, how errors are corrected (a new entry, not an edit).
Keep personal data off the shared record; store only business data.
3.ex: Lot 'R-0612-A' moves farm to packer to distributor to kitchen: four entries, each with time and quantity. A trace query returns the full path in under 10 seconds.
3.act: Build a spreadsheet prototype for one chain with at least 20 entries and run two trace queries.
3.std: Both queries return the full path; errors fixed by new entries.

4.title: Price the service and prove the saving
4.intro: Customers pay when savings beat the fee.
pts: Price per supplier or per site per month, plus set-up.
Compute customer benefit: recall cost avoided, labour saved on paperwork, premium for proven origin.
Compute your cost: cloud hosting, support, scanners, onboarding time.
Break-even = fixed cost / monthly margin per supplier.
4.ex: Price 2,400 a year per supplier; variable cost 900; margin 1,500. Fixed cost 9,000 a month is covered by 72 suppliers a year... that is 6 suppliers a month. Teaching figures in CAD.
4.act: Build the cost sheet and a customer saving case.
4.std: Units shown; saving case uses customer data.

5.title: Onboard suppliers and keep data clean
5.intro: The network only works if small suppliers can join easily.
pts: Offer phone-first capture and paper fallback with later entry.
Train in under one hour; provide a one-page guide in English and French.
Audit sample entries monthly against physical stock.
Set a rule for late or missing entries and follow it kindly.
5.ex: Pilot week 1: 62% of cases scanned; week 4: 91% after a quick guide and a helpline.
5.act: Run a 4-week capture test with three suppliers or a simulation.

6.title: Sell to buyers and partners
6.intro: Start where the pain is highest.
pts: Approach restaurant groups, grocers, distributors and certifiers.
Offer a 90-day pilot with a written success measure.
Show a live trace demo in under two minutes.
Track funnel: demos, pilots, paid.
6.act: Deliver a demo to five buyers.

7.title: Manage trust, security and misuse risk
7.intro: A record is only as true as what goes in.
pts: Garbage in, garbage out: a ledger proves an entry was made, not that it is true; add checks such as sensors and audits.
Secure keys and access; review accounts monthly.
Plan for supplier exit and data return.
Avoid hype: do not claim the ledger makes food safe.
7.ex: Risk: 'False origin entry | 3 x 5 | spot audits and sensor data | quality lead | monthly'.
7.std: Each row has owner and review date.

8.title: Pilot, review and scale
pts: Pilot 90 days on one product with five suppliers.
Measure trace time, scan rate and recall scope.
Stop rule: trace time over 1 minute after 60 days means redesign.
Plan the next chain.
8.ex: Result: trace time 8 seconds; scan rate 91%; proceed.
8.act: Run the pilot and present review.

quiz: When does a shared ledger beat a normal database?
When several parties must trust one record and none should control it.
What is the minimum trace record?
Lot code, product, quantity, date, from, to.
How are ledger errors corrected?
With a new entry, not an edit.
Why keep personal data off the ledger?
It cannot easily be erased and privacy law applies.
Does a ledger prove food is safe?
No. It proves an entry was made, not that it is true.
Name one check on entry truth.
Sensor data or spot audits.
What is break-even?
Fixed cost divided by margin per supplier.
Why offer a paper fallback?
Small suppliers can still join.
What does the pilot measure?
Trace time, scan rate and recall scope.
Why get advice before issuing a token?
Securities and money rules may apply.
